conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. Today I’d like to use a short, well-validated tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a set of 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; it just helps us see where you are emotionally so we can best support you. Everything you share stays confidential between you and the clinical team, and we’ll go at your pace. Ready to begin?

In the past week, have you generally been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I haven’t really felt like laughing much at all. Things that used to seem funny just kind of fall flat now. I can force a smile if someone tells a joke, but it doesn’t come naturally—it feels like work.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… that doesn’t sound right. I haven’t been able to laugh easily at all.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little outings or even just my favorite show, but lately nothing feels worth looking forward to. Everything just feels… flat, like I’m going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby fusses longer than usual, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m failing him somehow. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the nursery floor crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom over something so small.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when everything looks fine—he’s breathing, sleeping, no fever—I still feel this knot in my stomach that something bad is about to happen. I’ll lie in bed running through every awful scenario, sure I missed some danger sign.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits me out of nowhere. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly my heart’s racing, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something horrible is about to happen—even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small tasks. Feeding, changing, trying to nap when he naps—only the nap never really works because I’m listening for every squeak on the monitor. I keep telling myself millions of moms handle this, so why can’t I.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” and the guilt, and I can’t drift off. When I do finally sleep, I’m up every hour checking the bassinet or just staring at the ceiling.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start rolling—no real reason, just this steady sadness I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three or four times this week. Yesterday I sobbed in the shower because I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded at the park and felt like the world’s most useless mom. The tears just come and I can’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

Listening to you, I hear how heavy each day feels right now-how laughter and excitement seem distant, how even small tasks feel overwhelming, and how constant worry and self-blame have taken hold since your baby arrived. Your courage in sharing these feelings shows deep care for your child and a strong wish to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states inability to laugh and denies any ease with humor</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory joy and emotional flatness, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame that is disproportionate to the events (spilled milk, normal baby fussing), indicating the highest level of self-reproach.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant, pervasive anxiety ('pretty much all the time') with physical tension and intrusive catastrophic thoughts, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, dread) occurring unpredictably, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed most days, unable to manage basic tasks, and self-critical about not coping—matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to racing thoughts and anxiety, indicating sleep disturbance occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with uncontrollable crying, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week tied to feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your score of 26/30 places you well above the EPDS threshold of ≥14 that flags probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid anxiety. You describe core symptoms aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, insomnia, and recurrent anxiety/panic attacks. <quote>I'll lie in bed running through every awful scenario</quote> illustrates both insomnia and anxious rumination. Self-blame over routine infant-care events (<quote>I'm failing him somehow</quote>) signifies inappropriate guilt. <quote>Most days it feels like I'm drowning</quote> captures feeling overwhelmed. The combination of elevated depressive and anxiety items warrants urgent referral. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask your provider about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med>/other medications compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share your EPDS results openly so your clinician can complete a full diagnostic evaluation
4. Practice micro-breaks: accept help from partner/friends for 15-30 min rests to reduce overwhelm
5. Try brief breathing exercises (4-7-8) when <sym>panic symptoms</sym> surge
6. Keep a simple mood log to track changes for your next visit
7. Access local supports like <med>Postpartum Support International</med> Warmline 1-800-944-4PPD
8. If thoughts of self-harm ever arise, treat as an emergency and call 988 or 911
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-based):
- Anhedonia: marked loss of laughter and anticipatory enjoyment  
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, feelings of “heaviness”  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant-care events  
- Chronic, unprovoked anxiety (“knot in stomach,” racing heart, breathlessness) with sudden panic episodes  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “drowning” in daily tasks  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to ruminative worry  
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 negatively)

Pattern: High endorsement of core depressive and anxiety items; no safety concerns to self at present.

Screening significance:  
Score pattern consistent with probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Recommend formal clinical interview and further evaluation for diagnosis and care planning.
